newsitem.title: UK: Clarke to struggle to find substantial UK tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clarke to struggle to find substantial UK tax cuts.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, went into pre-budget meetings with policy advisers on Friday with economic data suggesting that he has little room to cut taxes.
But few economists expect him to avoid tax cuts completely in his November budget or bite the bullet and agree to an interest rate rise in the run-up to elections, which must be held by May 1997.
British finance ministers traditionally retreat with Treasury advisers into rural splendour at Dorneywood, the Chancellor's country residence, before the annual budget.
Clarke took his team down on Friday to thrash out budget details, with the meeting continuing on Saturday. The budget is set for November 26.
He has a number of options open to him, should he wish to cut taxes in an attempt to lure disaffected voters back to the fold. But his scope is limited.
"The Chancellor will spend this weekend at Dorneywood with a heavy heart," said Robert Barrie, UK economist at BZW.
He said the state of Britain's finances demanded fiscal and monetary tightening, not loosening. "But in the run-up to a general election, both will be left on hold."
Barrie said data this week crystallized Clarke's position, showing a tightening labour market feeding through into higher pay settlements and posing an inflationary threat.

A sharp 35,600 fall in unemployment in September, taking the total number of jobless to a five-and-a-half year low, was coupled with a pick-up in annual average earnings growth to 4.0 percent in July and August.
But, perhaps more importantly, September's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) -- the gap between government spending and revenues -- was well above forecasts at 3.4 billion stg.
The Treasury has already raised its forecast for the 1996/97 PSBR to 27.0 billion stg from 22.5 billion.
Now analysts fear that target could be missed. As a result, tax cuts, which would reduce government revenues, hardly seem a good idea, unless offset by spending cuts.
"PSBR figures were bad news for the Chancellor...ahead of Dorneywood," Barrie said. "They imply a headline deficit of 30 billion sterling rather than 27 billion."

Britain's public debt this year has been boosted by overshooting government spending. "The risks that spending cannot be controlled as tightly as planned ...imply a cautious budget," according to analysts at Goldman Sachs.
In their recent "Green Budget", produced with the Institute for Fiscal Studies, Goldman Sachs predicted modest tax cuts worth around three billion stg in November.
"The Chancellor will have to consider vociferous calls for tax reductions from his own party. It would be very surprising in this context not to see reductions in headline tax rates," it said.
The ruling Conservatives still trail by 20 points or more in opinion polls and are desperate for action to close the gap.

Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley, said Clarke could afford tax cuts of three billion stg at most and would endeavour to present his budget as a neutral one by reducing planned spending totals.
"We would hope to see slightly lower departmental spending totals, something Clarke conspicuously failed to deliver last year," he said.

Three billion stg in tax cuts could see one or two pence taken off the basic rate of income tax, now 24 percent. "He could also try to steal Labour's thunder by raising personal allowances and lowering the starting rate of income tax," Gardiner said.
The opposition Labour Party has pledged a starting rate of income tax of 10 percent in the long term. It is now 20 percent.
Industry groups are pleading for spending to be maintained in key areas, not sacrificed on the altar of tax cuts.
This week, the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) urged the Chancellor not to cut taxes or interest rates.
"Further reductions could cause undue stimulus to the economy, said Ian Peters, deputy director-general at the BCC.
Instead, he would prefer to see spending on education and the infrastructure maintained or increased in the budget.
But such a strategy would win few votes. "Let's get real," one analyst said. "It is a pre-election budget."
